item.title: Reading Marcus Aurelius With Feminine Pronouns
item.description:
Philosophy

Reading Marcus Aurelius With Feminine Pronouns

Catherine Yee's new version of "The Meditations."

Posted August 4, 2026

Key points
  • We are accustomed to examples of men and boys being protagonists in books and film.
  • It is interesting to realize how we maintain assumptions when we do not think we do.
  • Catherine Lee cleverly modifies "The Meditations" so we can see what adding feminine pronouns does for us.

The first time I was ever a student in a classroom where a female pronoun was used in a generic example, I literally startled and turned around to see who had walked into the lecture hall. I had assumed the professor was referencing an actual woman he was seeing.

But it turned out he was just experimenting with putting a woman in his example. "Imagine she then realizes the trolley is not going to stop."

Growing up, loving illustrated children's books, so many of the protagonists to identify with were boys. Researchers have counted, of course (imagine the work we would have to do without them), and found that the award-winning children's books from the 1940s to the 1960s featured boy or male protagonists at a two-to-one ratio.

And then, though I insist I was less influenced by film than it is commonly suggested we all are (we did not have cable or visit theaters much), the films of my era also featured male protagonists, and you would root for them, in all of their cases. The ratio of women or girl main characters to boys or men seems to have been the same as that for children's books.

What kind of impact could this have on us? Of course, that is very hard for them to assess, person by person. We obviously differ in our exposures and role models and commitments to fairness.

The philosopher Kate Manne, in her book Down Girl: The Logic of Misogyny, develops the concept of "himpathy," which we would experience whether or not we laughed along with the sexist films of the 1980s. It is the difference in the sympathy we have for men and boys compared to that we have for women and girls.

I think an easy test for this is how rattled you are depending on whether a boy or girl or woman or man starts crying.

Impacts like these are hard to recognize in reactions; we are just so accustomed to them. And of course the whole of our lives are difficult to assess as well; a good life is not made from how much sympathy (or himpathy) we garner. But to me, to realize how we ourselves maintain assumptions when we do not think we do is so interesting.

A more sustained test of this is to read Catherine Yee's revision of George Chrystal's older translation of Marcus Aurelius's Meditations. She replaced masculine references with "feminine and neutral forms" throughout, preserving the rest.

Will it not matter to you? Or will that bother you each time you see it?

Likely you will not nearly jump out of your seat as I did first hearing "she" used in a classroom example, because we have changed our view on women's roles in even our lifetimes. But Yee's clever switch will still surely get you thinking about what you are bringing to the ancient text, how very much that is.

And what a good philosophical and Stoic exercise that would be.

item.title: Can We Teach Kids to Be Kinder?
item.description:
Child Development

Can We Teach Kids to Be Kinder?

Can kindness be taught? Developmental psychology suggests that the answer is yes.

Posted August 4, 2026

Key points
  • Kindness is shaped not only by genes but also by children's experiences.
  • A randomized controlled trial found that a school kindness program improved multiple student outcomes.
  • The benefits extended beyond kindness to happiness, behaviour, relationships, and learning.

Kindness is typically understood as "actions intended to benefit others, usually at some cost" to the actor. Research has found that kindness-related traits emerge early in infancy and continue to develop throughout childhood. Individual differences in kindness—and related traits such as altruism, benevolence, and compassion—are partly due to genetic differences, but largely due to differences in children's experiences outside the home.

School-Based Social and Emotional Learning

Schools are one possible source of these experiences, and school-based social and emotional learning (SEL) programs are one attempt to provide them. A growing body of evidence suggests that they work. Recent meta-analyses have found that SEL programs have small-to-moderate positive effects on prosocial behaviour, as well as on well-being, attention, behaviour, peer relationships, and academic performance.

We recently conducted a randomized controlled trial of our own SEL program, Learn Kind, which is currently taught by more than 1,000 teachers to more than 100,000 students each year.

Learn Kind is an eight-part kindness-based curriculum for students in grades K–8. Rather than simply telling children to "be nice," the program treats kindness as an object of scientific inquiry. Students are invited to act as "student scientists," discovering for themselves what increases kindness and the effects it can have. The curriculum covers topics including the science of kindness, compassion, cooperation, self-kindness, and the relationship between helping others and happiness. It also includes an experiential component in which students perform acts of kindness and record their effects on themselves and others, testing the hypothesis that helping others makes people happier.

To evaluate the program, 50 teachers, reporting on more than 1,000 students, were randomly assigned either to teach Learn Kind during the autumn term (the treatment group) or to wait until the spring term (the waitlist control group). Teachers rated their students' kindness (using a simple kindness grade of A, B, C, D, or F), prosociality, emotions, attention, behaviour, peer relationships, happiness, and academic performance in mathematics and reading.

Study Findings

The study found significant improvements across a wide range of outcomes. Most strikingly, students in the Learn Kind group improved by approximately one full letter grade in kindness, moving from an average rating of C to B. Compared with the control group, they were also rated as happier, more prosocial, better behaved, and more attentive; had stronger peer relationships; and showed modest improvements in mathematics and reading. Across all outcomes, the average effect size was d = 0.34.

Importantly, these improvements largely persisted. When students were assessed again three months later, gains in kindness, happiness, behaviour, peer relationships, and academic performance were still evident.

Benchmarking these results against previous evaluations suggests that Learn Kind ranks in approximately the top quartile of SEL programs.

These findings add to growing evidence that kindness is not simply an inborn disposition but a skill that can be developed through experience. More broadly, they suggest that well-designed educational programs can improve not only kindness itself but also children's social, emotional, and academic development.

We hope this is only the beginning. Our plan is to expand Learn Kind by incorporating classroom experiments exploring additional virtues, such as gratitude, generosity, fairness, and honesty. This would create a "virtual laboratory" in which thousands of student scientists contribute to the psychological science of character development, with the potential to identify ever more effective interventions that help kids become kinder and happier.

item.title: Clinical Wisdom: Quintessential Secrets of Psychotherapy
item.description:
Wisdom

Clinical Wisdom: Quintessential Secrets of Psychotherapy

What do we mean by "clinical wisdom," and why do we need it today?

Posted August 4, 2026

Key points
  • Clinical wisdom is indirectly or directly conveyed from psychotherapist to patient in therapy.
  • Clinical wisdom contains practical information about living meaningfully, productively, and creatively.
  • Conveying clinical wisdom is not the same as providing advice.
Freud's psychoanalytic couch
Source: ROBERT HUFFSTUTTER / Wikimedia Commons, Creative Commons Attribution 2.0

In Part 2 of this series, I defined the term "clinical wisdom" and how it can be employed in psychotherapy, as, for example, to begin with, in the management of expectations about treatment on the parts of both therapist and patient or client. Here, in Part 5, I discuss some other examples of what I mean by "clinical wisdom" in terms of what it is—and what it is not.

Conveying Clinical Wisdom Is Not Giving Advice

Here is a little secret that some patients (and psychotherapists) might find surprising: Clinical wisdom is not about advice-giving. It is, for the most part, never conveyed or communicated by telling patients what not to do, what to do, or how to do it. Psychotherapists seldom (if ever) proffer such direct advice per se to patients regarding how they should live their lives or what major decisions to make. It would be presumptuous, counterproductive, grandiose, authoritarian, and, arguably, unethical to do so. This is always the patient's responsibility, and theirs alone, which is one example of the clinical wisdom existential therapists consistently try to encourage, communicate, and convey to them in therapy.

Most people enter therapy with the conscious or unconscious expectation or wish that the therapist will, like a parent, teacher, priest, rabbi, etc., or, for that matter, close friend or confidante, counsel or concretely advise them, if not overtly tell them what to do with their lives, believing that this is our professional role. A form of positive transference to a perceived authority figure. But clearly, this is one of the major misconceptions people (and some therapists or counselors) bring to therapy. Yes, it is true that, as Rollo May (1991) observes, "therapists belong to a strange profession. It is partly religion. . . .We cannot deny that we . . . therapists deal with people's moral and spiritual questions and that we fill the role of father [or mother] confessor as part of our armamentarium, as [originally] shown in Freud's position behind and unseen by the person confessing."

Indeed, this confessional and unburdening quality of psychotherapy, like the ancient healing rite of confession in the Catholic church, may play a significant part in what actually makes therapy therapeutic. Nevertheless, we as psychotherapists do not want to advise or counsel our clients or patients how to conduct their lives, what to value or believe in, what political party to vote for, and which choices to make but, rather, encourage and support them in discovering for themselves their own intrinsic freedom and responsibility, despite the inevitable discomfort, doubts, and anxiety of doing so. Having said that, this is an admittedly extraordinarily challenging therapeutic stance to maintain, since the clinician's own conscious and unconscious beliefs, biases, prejudices, values, preferences, traits, etc. permeate our presumably neutral clinical persona despite our best efforts to prevent them from "leaking" out.

Helping Without Helping; Caring Without Caring

It is, if truth be told, what happens within this crucial therapeutic alliance, container, or what Jungians refer to as sacred temenos that really matters. (See Part 6 of this series.) While being supportive and caring, we as clinicians must allow our patients to wrestle with these spiritual and existential conundrums on their own without telling them what to do one way or the other (i.e., without interference or rescuing). Here I am reminded of a dream one of Jung's patients recounted to him in which she was buried up to her neck in a pit of burning embers and desperately begging the nearby Dr. Jung to help her out of it. Instead, in the dream, Jung approached his suffering patient, placed his hand gently on her shoulder, and firmly pushed her even further down into the fiery hole, saying, "Not out, but through." This is itself a core kind of clinical wisdom. How to care but, at the same time, not care. To help, but not help. To practice a type of Buddhistic detachment from both the therapeutic process and outcome while remaining nonetheless fully committed and empathically present. Certainly, the psychotherapist, who undeniably does possess some expertise and authority, can and sometimes must make certain clinical recommendations or, in some cases, prescriptions to the patient, but even then, it must be remembered and emphasized that the person is free and responsible to accept or reject such recommendations as they will and must be permitted to do so.

So, transmitting clinical wisdom is something very different than telling someone how to live their life, which fosters dependency rather than independence and self-reliance, something antithetical to the therapy project. Moreover, everyone in the patient's circle has already provided practical, well-intentioned (but typically unsolicited) advice such as, for instance, stop drinking, meditate, start dating, etc., to no avail. Such seemingly good advice suffers from three shortcomings: First, the advice tends typically to be totally generic and not tailored to the specific situation or person; second, the person receiving the advice may not have requested it nor recognize what makes it necessary or advisable; and third, the recipient of said advice would need to consciously choose to follow it consistently in opposition to their neurotic tendencies not to. It can be a fine line. In psychotherapy, the focus is not on providing advice, much of which the patient has probably heard before, but rather on addressing their resistance, unwillingness, refusal, fear, or inability to accept and put it into practice and what prevents that from happening. And, much more importantly, to learn to listen to themselves rather than others, including the therapist, to trust and courageously follow their own inner daimon (see Diamond, 1996), voice, guidance, instincts, or direction with as much integrity and authenticity as practically possible.

Will, Freedom, Responsibility, and Clinical Wisdom

Thus, when we speak about "clinical wisdom," we are not talking about explicitly or implicitly advising or counseling our patients or clients but drawing upon and bringing to bear indirectly, subtly, or implicitly, or, in some situations, sharing openly, some of these esoteric secrets with them for their consideration. To some extent, psychotherapy conveys clinical wisdom to the client or patient partly in the form of valuable psychological, philosophical, or spiritual information and knowledge relevant to their present predicament. But ultimately, as with solicited or unsolicited advice, it is purely the patient's responsibility (and a direct expression of their own free will) to choose how or whether to accept and apply such clinical wisdom to themselves and their own situations as they see fit. This recognition of the inherent inefficacy and, in some cases, counterproductivity of giving patients or clients advice—due to the person rebelling against or resisting being told what to do or not to do by some external authority figure or perhaps following the advice and then blaming or crediting the clinician for the outcome instead of themselves—may itself mark the beginning of some real clinical wisdom.
